title: Microsoft says AI rival Anthropic could have 'disastrous impact' on humanity
description: Microsoft's head of AI has warned Anthropic's approach to training its AI model Claude could have a "disastrous impact on the wellbeing of humanity".M
body: Microsoft's head of AI has warned Anthropic's approach to training its AI model Claude could have a "disastrous impact on the wellbeing of humanity".Mustafa Suleyman said his rival risked creating something "impossible" to control by treating it like a human - including by telling it it "may be conscious" and was "deserving of independent agency"."We must not sleepwalk our way into a decision we later come to bitterly regret," he wrote.The comments are the latest in a series of stark warnings from the AI industry on the possible dangers of the technology. The BBC has contacted Anthropic for comment."AIs are not conscious," he wrote. "They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations."They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions, and accomplish goals set by humans."In a lengthy essay, Suleyman praised Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and his team for being "thoughtful, principled, and intellectually honest people" - but nevertheless questioned the company.He heavily criticised Anthropic for teaching its AI to have human-like qualities, a practice known as anthropomorphising, which he said made it seem as though Claude had its own desires, values and sense of self.But he argued "consciousness is biological", saying there is "no evidence to suggest that AI is conscious".As well as calling for a debate on the issue, Suleyman said greater transparency around how AI systems are trained and evaluated was needed.This, he said, included independent scrutiny of AI behaviour and stronger tools to monitor and control the technology.Dame Wendy Hall, professor of Computer Science at the University of Southampton, described the comments as "the sort of conversation we need to be having internationally", contrasting it with the "histrionics" from some AI companies which she said only served to "scare everyone".

schema.headline: Microsoft says AI rival Anthropic could have 'disastrous impact' on humanity

title: Eight German state premiers back Merz amid speculation over his future
description: The leaders of eight German states have backed the nation's chancellor amid growing speculation about his political future.The premiers - all of whom
body: The leaders of eight German states have backed the nation's chancellor amid growing speculation about his political future.The premiers - all of whom are part of Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) - wrote that restoring trust in their party lay in "listening ​and taking political action, not in debates ​over personnel".Merz, who has only held the post for 16 months, is facing poor approval ratings while the anti-immigration, far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is surging, prompting questions about whether he is an electoral liability.He has vowed to carry on but two more state elections on Sunday have been seen as a key test of his leadership.Rumours of a "Kanzlertausch" - or "Chancellor swap" - have been around for months, but they have increased since the conservative CDU tumbled to a distant second behind the AfD in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt at the start of September.The AfD shot up to 43.8% of the vote while the CDU plummeted to 17.2%, marking the first time since World War Two that a far-right party has come close to controlling a German state.It is still three seats short of an outright majority and the major parties would not enter into a coalition with the AfD, though it could seek to form a minority government.Merz came out fighting after the loss, describing the AfD - which wants to rebuild ties with Russia - as a "destructive force" whose migration policy amounted to an "ethnic cleansing" of skilled workers.The AfD responded to his remarks by saying it was filing a defamation complaint against the chancellor over what it described as "baseless" and "disgusting" claims.The chancellor's abrasive communication style and personal unpopularity - with just 14% thinking he is right for the job, according to a recent Bild poll - have raised questions about his viability as leader of both Germany and the CDU.The CDU's eight state premiers wrote, however, that "now more than ever, ⁠Germany's political landscape needs stability"."Our country will continue to need a stable and effective federal government with its own majority in the Bundestag [German parliament]," said the leaders of Schleswig-Holstein, Saxony, Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia, Berlin and North Rhine-Westphalia.It comes after Markus Söder, the premier of Bavaria and leader of the CDU's sister party the CSU, stood by Merz.An unnamed party source told news agency Reuters that CDU officials will meet on Sunday to co-ordinate the party's response to the results of that day's state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-West Pomerania - where the AfD is poised for further gains and the CDU for further losses.However, the race is far more evenly split in the German capital than it was in Saxony-Anhalt, with the CDU and Die Linke (The Left) vying for first place, and the AfD and Greens not far behind, according to polls.In Mecklenburg-West Pomerania, polls put the AfD ahead of the centre-left SPD but likely well short of an outright majority.The worst-case scenario for Merz would be for the CDU to lose power in Berlin and not get enough votes to even have a presence in Mecklenburg-West Pomerania's parliament.Unlike in the UK, Germany is not well-versed in replacing its leader mid-term, though Merz could, in theory, be pressured to resign or face a vote of no confidence, though many regard that outcome as unlikely.No one within the CDU has yet said they were willing to challenge Merz, but the speculation about his future has led to several names - including Söder, North Rhine-Westphalia premier Hendrik Wüst and German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt - being touted as potential successors.Even before Merz had officially been made chancellor, he managed to rally support for a massive €500bn ($547bn; £420bn) defence infrastructure fund, with his straight-talking style and focus on European security earning him plaudits on the world stage.But it took him three attempts to become CDU leader and he then lost an initial vote to become chancellor despite technically having sufficient votes through a coalition deal with the SPD. It was a first in post-war Germany.This suggests that he has a history of struggling to appeal to even those within his own ranks - and that he may be unlikely to let go of a job he has long coveted.

schema.headline: Eight German state premiers back Merz amid speculation over his future

title: Part-human part-mouse brain developed in science breakthrough
description: The aim of this ethically complicated breakthrough was to better understand the biology of brain disorders for which there are currently no effective
body: The aim of this ethically complicated breakthrough was to better understand the biology of brain disorders for which there are currently no effective treatments.Some conditions cannot be studied in a mouse, simply because rodents do not develop some of the brain disorders that we do. As lead researcher Prof Sergiu Pașca from Stanford University explained in a press conference, psychiatry has "one of the lowest success rates for clinical trials"."Even drugs that actually make it to clinical trial - that seem to be working really well in animal models - fail dramatically in clinic," he said in a press conference. "That tells us we're missing a lot of information about human biology and capturing that will be essential."The Stanford researchers said that, for some complex conditions, including epilepsy, autism and cerebral palsy, it has the potential to be "transformative".Pașca said: "Here we have a new model that allows us to actually capture aspects of human brain function in a way that has not been possible before."The human brain is made up of billions of cells, interconnected in millions of circuits, making it difficult to understand its development and what exactly is happening – at the cellular level - when things go wrong.While this research is not the first time human neurons have been implanted in laboratory rodents, external, these scientists took that approach to a new level.First, they genetically-engineered mice to develop almost none of their own cerebral cortex – that is the outer layer of the brain sometimes referred to as "grey matter". It handles higher-level thinking, memory and senses.The researchers then used skin cells taken from humans and "reprogrammed" them, so they grew into pieces of brain-like tissue. These are structures called organoids – they are not whole brains grown in dishes, more collections of connected, living cells.When these organoids were implanted into the mouse brain the cells divided and organised themselves into the animal's existing brain circuitry, connecting with the rest of the mouse's brain and spinal cord.The cortex of the implanted mice is not perfect - normal cortex forms organised, structured layers. And as neuroscientist Dr Ilary Allodi put it, scans of these human-mouse brains look "a bit messy".  After a few months though, the human cells started to look and function like the outer layer of the mouse's brain.About six months after the surgery, scientists put the mice through some basic behavioural tests  - observing them as they moved around a small table-top arena.Pașca said they performed "largely as [the normal] mice did"."They don't have any enhancement," he added.Dr Sarah Chan, a reader in bioethics at the University of Edinburgh who was not involved in this research, told BBC News there was "no indication that what's being created here are mice that can think like humans, or a human brain in a mouse body."But she said the study "prompts us to think about what it might mean when we start changing animal cognition"."How can we know what it's like to be one of these mice? And how do we take account of that in the ways that we treat laboratory animals," she added.Dr Ilary Allodi, a neuroscientist from St Andrews University, who was not involved in the research, said the work the scientists had done was "very impressive".In particular, Allodi pointed to the fact that cell types that are found only in human and other primate brains - not in the brains of mice – spontaneously formed in the implanted mice. "You're keeping the human program inside the mouse environment – like the mouse is an incubator," she told BBC News.These mice, which the researchers said are engineered and reared under strict ethical and welfare guidelines, will most likely be used in a small number of labs for studies of a few, very specific brain disorders. Prof James Ainge, a neuroscientist who is also at St Andrews University, pointed out that while the development was technically very impressive, these mice could be "of limited use".This, he said, was partly due to the "ethical issues of raising living human brain tissue in a mouse and what that would mean for the experience of the animal".Neuroscientists who study the human brain, Allodi pointed out, all struggle with the same limitations. "We try to understand human disease, and what we have is mice, cells that live on a plate, and neural networks on a computer."So this is a new avenue."

schema.headline: Part-human part-mouse brain developed in science breakthrough

title: Sunny, Barack Obama's 'fiery and gorgeous' dog, dies
description: The Obamas' beloved pet dog Sunny has died after 13 years with the family, Barack Obama has announced. "Yesterday, we lost a cherished member of our f
body: The Obamas' beloved pet dog Sunny has died after 13 years with the family, Barack Obama has announced. "Yesterday, we lost a cherished member of our family," the former US president wrote on X, describing her as a loyal dog who was "pretty much perfect" and always by their side.The family had two Portuguese Water Dogs in the White House. They got Sunny at the beginning of Obama's second presidential term in 2013. Sunny met many high-profile visitors while Obama was president, from foreign dignitaries to Pope Francis.Their other dog, Bo, joined the family in 2009 as a gift for daughters Sasha and Malia to help them settle into the White House. Bo died in 2021.Obama said that when Sunny joined the family they "immediately fell in love". He described her as "full of boundless energy", saying she leapt over the hedges on the South Lawn like they weren't even there.Sunny most enjoyed "having us run around with her, roll on the floor with her, or have her belly rubbed for as long as we were willing", he wrote."She loved the girls, even if they were pestering her when she was napping. She loved our team, and would often follow them around, helping them on the job."Obama added that Sunny was "a loud and sloppy drinker" who hated getting wet. "For thirteen years, she would be by our side – always loyal, always sweet, always ready for adventure, still fiery and gorgeous till the very end of her days."He said the family would miss her terribly and that she was now with her "big brother" Bo.

schema.headline: Sunny, Barack Obama's 'fiery and gorgeous' dog, dies

title: Andy Burnham and his chancellor have a battle on their hands
description: Today's inflation figures underscore that the economy is the biggest challenge facing Andy Burnham.It is only 42 days until John Healey's first Budget
body: Today's inflation figures underscore that the economy is the biggest challenge facing Andy Burnham.It is only 42 days until John Healey's first Budget, and there is increasingly apparent concern at all levels of the government and Labour Party about how that Budget can – or, as it may prove, cannot – substantiate Burnham's rhetoric about offering the biggest change in British politics in 40 years.Much of the tricky economic environment, yes, is driven by global factors including the persistence, and to some degree worsening, of the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine.And the AI boom pushing up borrowing costs is another issue affecting many countries.But there are clearly domestic factors particular to Britain, and on that front it was very striking to hear the former Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane telling LBC on Tuesday that without signs of cuts to public spending "the markets now suspect that this is a traditional tax and spend socialist government with better TikTok videos".From somebody who at times has informally advised Burnham's operation, that will sting, not least because a similar criticism has been voiced in recent weeks by the prominent economist Lord O'Neill – another sometime adviser.The prime minister gave a direct response to Haldane, saying: "That doesn't tell the story. We are not that."He identified "putting digital ID on hold" as an example of how he had already "taken difficult decisions in this job in relation to reprioritising government spending" and vowed to continue to "take difficult decisions to make sure the economy remains on track".Digital ID is a striking choice of example. Burnham announced that he was abandoning the scheme in the days before he became prime minister so that he could focus on policies affecting the everyday cost of living. But the spending was then, within the new government's first few days, re-allocated to cut VAT on household electricity bills.So in that sense it was not a reduction in public spending, just a reprioritisation. And in any case, the former cabinet minister Darren Jones criticised Burnham at the time on the grounds that the government had not yet allocated the money for digital ID.Certainly the signs from Healey's first major speech as chancellor last week were that he wants to reassure the markets, promising to "control public spending" and praising Rachel Reeves for beginning to "recover Britain's fiscal discipline".Burnham and Healey would hardly be the first PM-chancellor double act to adopt different tones and emphasise different priorities in their public appearances. As a junior minister at the Treasury almost 25 years ago, Healey was engaged in the question of how to boost growth around the country, long before it became central to Burnham's vision for Britain.But there are people in government who are beginning to wonder whether their economic visions are quite as aligned as expected. "It's what everyone is thinking and some of us are vocalising," one government source said.There are also those who fear the adverse political consequences of a Labour government seeking to go out of its way to demonstrate its fiscal credibility. Arguably that was behind the removal of the Winter Fuel Allowance for most pensioners as one of Sir Keir Starmer's first acts, an early factor in his political demise.For Labour's political opponents, all this amounts to a question of whether the prime minister is willing to disappoint his own MPs. Yet it's worth remembering that with winter fuel the frustration in parliament was primarily caused by the furious reaction of Labour MPs' constituents.Arguably this presents a more fundamental tension: are the kinds of policies needed to soothe the markets politically deliverable given Labour's electoral coalition and its need to shore up the 'progressive' vote?The Budget is only six weeks away and will be the first and most important sign of the new government's answer to that question.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham and his chancellor have a battle on their hands

title: 'Putney pusher' suspect found dead at home
description: Image source, Central NewsImage caption, Nicholas Brandram, pictured in 2013, was found dead on TuesdayByEllie PriceNews correspondent and James W Kel
body: Image source, Central NewsImage caption, Nicholas Brandram, pictured in 2013, was found dead on TuesdayByEllie PriceNews correspondent and James W KellyLondonUpdated 3 hours agoThe man suspected of pushing a woman into the path of a bus during a run on Putney Bridge in west London in 2017, has been found dead at his home.Nicholas Brandram, 44, was under investigation in the so-called "Putney pusher" case, after CCTV went viral showing just how close the woman came to be run over by the 430 bus, in a seemingly unprovoked attack.He was arrested in June this year on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. Last week, the Metropolitan Police confirmed he had been released under investigation.The banker was found dead in his home on Tuesday evening. The Met said his death was being treated as "unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious".Figure caption, The incident happened nine years agoA spokesperson for the force said officers attended the property in Chiswick alongside paramedics "after a man was found unresponsive"."Sadly, a 44-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next-of-kin have been informed," they said. Brandram, who served as a Captain in the Scots Guards in Afghanistan, was working more recently in private banking for HSBC.He is a distant relative of European royalty - his grandmother was Princess Katherine of Greece, and the late Duke of Edinburgh, Prince Philip, was his father's godfather.'Quick reactions'While in police custody in June over the Putney Bridge incident, Brandram was also arrested on suspicion of drug possession.Shortly after the incident in 2017, investigating officer Sgt Mat Knowles said: "It was only due to the superb quick reactions of the bus driver that she was not hit by the vehicle."Bus driver Oliver Salbris told the Sunday Times following the incident: "If I hadn't swerved, I would have smashed her head."It was reflex. The consequences would have been terrible for her – and for me."Detectives identified more than 50 people of interest following the incident. The Met had initially closed its investigation in 2018 after three men had been arrested and released without charge.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: EU chief backs plan for Canada to become 'associate member'
description: The president of the European Commission has backed proposals for Canada to become the EU's first "associate member".Ursula von der Leyen told the Eur
body: The president of the European Commission has backed proposals for Canada to become the EU's first "associate member".Ursula von der Leyen told the European Parliament on Wednesday she wanted to work on "opening the door" for Canada, which would involve closer ties on various key sectors.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney last week spoke of seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU. The country currently faces tense relations with the US, compounded by an intensifying dispute over trade.Without mentioning US President Donald Trump by name, von der Leyen said offering Canada some sort of EU membership was "not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength". She added: "Partnerships are a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system".Carney was in attendance at the annual key note speech in Strasbourg, and is due to address the parliament on Thursday.Trade talks between Canada and the US collapsed last month, sparking a series of new tariff measures. Trump's repeated talk of making Canada a "51st state" has also helped to fuel the feud between the North American neighbours.Von der Leyen told the EU's State of the Union address that the bloc and Canada "see the world with the same eyes", including on topics ranging from AI, to climate change and geopolitics."And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defence, on raw materials and on supply chains. But above all... Europe and Canada believe in democracy."She did not give specific details on how any Canadian membership would work, but listed manufacturing, technology, AI, defence, energy, critical minerals and economic security as key areas for cooperation.Both she and other European leaders have found a reliable ally in Carney as they deal with similar problems.In particular, they have faced Trump's aggressive use of tariffs and his threat to annex Greenland which is a sovereign territory of EU member Denmark.But "associate membership" of the EU does not currently exist and the process, if agreed, could take years.Earlier this year, Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested - to a mixed reaction - that Ukraine could be granted this new status.Some countries in the western Balkans including Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Serbia are already on the long road towards full EU membership.In Eastern Europe, Georgia and Moldova are also applying.Ten of the bloc's 27 members are yet to ratify a free-trade agreement struck with Ottawa nearly a decade ago, and some capitals would prefer to build on existing defence and trade agreements rather than create a new form of membership for Canada.Setting out the EU's political and policy priorities for year ahead, von der Leyen also proposed the formation of a European Security Council, which would include the UK and Ukraine, amid an ongoing threat to the continent from Russia. "For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent, with partners like Canada, Norway, Ukraine, the United Kingdom and others involved," she said in the wide-ranging address."This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play. This is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality."Calls for such a body have been growing since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.It was initially a French-German conception but more countries have shown support, particularly as Trump has questioned the Nato military alliance. Other nations worry such a council could unhelpfully rival Nato.Von der Leyen said the EU was "strengthening our work with Nato" and that expanded defence spending would be "fully aligned" with the alliance.But at the core of such a security council would be the ability to trigger an emergency meeting if one member felt under threat, similar to Nato's Article 4.The EU chief said it would be a "mechanism to flank" Article 4, a term that could be interpreted as complementing Nato functions or - if taken in a military context - bypassing them.Alongside global threats, von der Leyen also said many European families were worried about the cost of living, and the "dizzying speed of change" of technology and its impacts on jobs and society.Other proposals included inviting the world's largest AI labs for talks on how to support industry efforts to pace the frontier, as well as slashing bureaucracy for businesses in the EU. Plans to curb social media use among children, including banning platforms for under 13s, were also put forward. Under the proposal, children aged 13 to 15 would only be able to set up social media accounts which are supervised by parents.A new emergency tool to help countries better deal with mass migration movements following the deadly influx of migrants to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in July would also be outlined.The pledge chimes with the message of European politicians on the right and hard right who have gained support in recent years for proposing a tougher approach.Some of them called the mass attempt to enter the EU through Ceuta an "invasion" and argued asylum rules should be suspended to deal with such a crisis.Von der Leyen said the new emergency tool would "only be triggered under a strictly defined set of criteria" and for a specific period of time, and that fundamental rights would be protected.Human rights groups worry such a move would see vulnerable people, including women and children, turned back and denied the protection afforded to them under international law.

schema.headline: EU chief backs plan for Canada to become 'associate member'

title: How escalating Saudi oil crisis could drive up prices everywhere
description: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondent, BBC VerifyGlobal energy prices have spiked alarmingly again, drive
body: Image source, Bloomberg via Getty ImagesByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondent, BBC VerifyGlobal energy prices have spiked alarmingly again, driven largely in recent days by the escalating conflict between Yemen's Houthis and Saudi Arabia causing chaos for the oil industry.Petrol and diesel costs have risen rapidly in most countries while the wholesale price of natural gas - used for heating homes and generating electricity - has almost doubled in the UK and Europe since July.There are growing concerns of another inflationary shock on the world economy, which could cause interest rates to rise, increase mortgage costs and raise the price of almost everything in the shops including food.So what is behind this latest surge - and what are the implications for the world economy?Petrol, diesel and gas prices are risingThe global oil price is currently above $108 (£80) per barrel, up from $70 (£52) in June 2026 - a roughly 50% increase.This has contributed to average petrol prices in the UK going above 170p a litre, the highest since 2022 and up from 150p in July.As a result of the near-doubling of UK natural gas costs alongside this the domestic price cap set by energy regulator Ofgem is forecast to rise by 25% in January next year - or about £440 a year for a typical household.In the US, the cost of a gallon (3.8 litres) of petrol has risen from $3.80 (£2.82) in July to $4.32 (£3.20), according to the AAA Gas Prices index.Diesel prices have hit a record level in the US of more than $6 (£4.46) a gallon, higher even than after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.What's pushing up prices?Analysts say the main driver has been a reduction in global oil and gas supplies.Before the US-Israeli war with Iran began in late February, about 20% of both global oil products and liquefied natural gas supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway connecting the Gulf and the Arabian Sea.This flow of energy collapsed after February due to Iranian attacks on commercial shipping and the energy facilities of US allies in the Gulf as well as a US blockade of Iran's ports.After the war began, Saudi Arabia stepped up the use of its East-West pipeline - which according to maritime intelligence firm Kpler has a capacity of 3.6 million barrels per day - to export oil via the Red Sea, rather than the Strait of Hormuz.But the pipeline was forced to shut down after it was attacked by drones on Friday, which Saudi Arabia has blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq.The Houthis separately attacked several Saudi oil facilities with drones and missiles last week, causing fires which led to operations being temporarily halted.Neil Quilliam of Chatham House said the pipeline could be closed for up to eight weeks for repair - although US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told broadcaster CNBC on Tuesday it will start operating again "very soon".And despite the US government insisting fuel is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz in roughly pre-war volumes, most independent analysts judge that the waterway remains significantly obstructed.Before the war around 21 million barrels per day of oil and oil products were passing through the Strait of Hormuz, according to the US Energy Information Administration.But Kpler estimated this had fallen to about 8.6 million barrels per day by the end of August.Over the past two weeks, the Houthis in Yemen have captured strategic territory from Saudi-backed pro-government forces close to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, another trade chokepoint at the southern tip of the Red Sea which was the transit point for about 5% of global oil supplies before February.About 5% of the global oil supply also normally leaves the Red Sea through the north, via the Suez Canal and a pipeline across Egypt to the Mediterranean.The global market oil price is rising over concerns these shipping arteries could, like Hormuz, be even more severely disrupted by Iran and its proxies.Before the Houthis recent advances on the south-west coast of Yemen the group declared in July it was enforcing a naval blockade of Saudi ships and ports. It said it will not attack vessels from other countries passing through the Red Sea.US President Donald Trump has said "the world's diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran".Analysts say the conflict - including Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries - has put pressure on diesel prices as Russia is the world's second largest diesel exporter.But most judge the bigger cause of the recent energy price spike has been the expanding regional conflict in the Middle East.What does it mean for the global economy?Economists say that higher global energy prices - if sustained - usually lead to even higher prices for households and weaker economic growth, which translates into lower incomes and wages for people.The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has estimated that a sustained 10% increase in oil prices increases global inflation by 0.4% and reduces global GDP growth by up to 0.2%.The Bank of England has estimated that a 10% increase in global oil price increases the UK inflation rate by 0.5% in the near-term and reduces UK GDP growth by about 0.4%.The rise in the global oil price since June is about five times larger than in the scenario used by the IMF and the Bank of England in their economic models to assess the impact of rising oil prices.However, it is possible that the global oil price could drop again if there is a peace agreement between the US and Iran.After a preliminary deal was signed between the two warring parties in June, the oil price temporarily fell  sharply to pre-war levels, having gone as high as $120 a barrel.Additional reporting by Nicholas Barrett and Joshua Cheetham

schema.headline: How escalating Saudi oil crisis could drive up prices everywhere

title: At least 21 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses
description: At least 21 people have been killed, including eight children, after a war-damaged building collapsed in the Gaza Strip overnight, rescuers and medics
body: At least 21 people have been killed, including eight children, after a war-damaged building collapsed in the Gaza Strip overnight, rescuers and medics say.Witnesses told the BBC that the six-storey building in Gaza City's Tal al-Hawa area had been left tilting dangerously to one side after an Israeli strike more than a year ago. Displaced families had lived inside because they were desperate, they said.UN and Egyptian teams joined the search for survivors, which was slow due to a lack of equipment. Initially, rescuers from the Hamas-run Civil Defence agency had to use their bare hands.On Wednesday afternoon, they said they had ended the operation after taking 45 injured people to hospitals.Sherif, whose sister was killed, said: "They couldn't find a tent or somewhere to live."This was the last place they could turn to, despite the danger. They were aware that it would likely end in tragedy. A lack of resources drove them towards certain death."The head of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Gaza office, Alessandro Mrakic, told reporters at the scene on Wednesday morning that "the situation... is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed".He also warned that approximately 400 other war-damaged buildings across Gaza were at imminent risk of collapse, particularly as winter approaches."We need support, most importantly with machinery, equipment, among others. Our colleagues here don't have [engine] oil and spare parts to continue to work with all the equipment that is still in Gaza."The UN's humanitarian relief co-ordinator, Ramiz Alakbarov, said he was "devastated" by the reports of the building collapse."No-one should have to risk their life simply to find a safe place to shelter," he said.He also urged Israeli authorities to approve deliveries to Gaza of heavy machinery for rescue operations, as well as tents, tarpaulins and other non-food items for displaced people ahead of the winter rains.Israel says its restrictions are meant to keep equipment out of the hands of Palestinian armed groups that could also have military uses.An estimated 80% of all structures in Gaza have been destroyed or damaged during the war between Israel and Hamas, according to the UN.More than 1.9 million people - about 90% of the territory's population - have been displaced, many of them multiple times, and 1.2 million of them are currently living in tents or makeshift shelters, it says.The UN has warned that the humanitarian situation in Gaza remains dire despite the ceasefire agreed last October, as Israeli air strikes and other attacks continue to hit populated areas, causing casualties and property damage and driving further displacement.On Tuesday, Israeli air strikes killed at least five Palestinians, including two children and a Hamas commander, according to health officials and Hamas sources.The Israeli military said it killed a Hamas commander in southern Gaza and another fighter in the north. In both cases, a child was also reportedly killed.Separately, the British charity Medical Aid for Palestinians said that a patient was killed by an Israeli drone at a health centre it supports in Jabalia in northern Gaza. A spokesperson for the Israeli military told the BBC it was not aware of such an incident.The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Since then, more than 73,790 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

schema.headline: At least 21 killed after war-damaged Gaza building collapses

title: Photos show widespread damage at US sites from Iranian attacks
description: Images showing widespread damage to multiple US sites in the Middle East from Iranian strikes have been obtained by the BBC's US partner CBS.The photo
body: Images showing widespread damage to multiple US sites in the Middle East from Iranian strikes have been obtained by the BBC's US partner CBS.The photos, provided by active military personnel, show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings.The undated photos were taken at US bases and sites in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait.One member of the military, who was not named by CBS, said: "This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public."We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face."The White House referred the BBC to US Central Command. Centcom did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The photos, which have not been independently verified by the BBC, were published the day after a report from the Pentagon's watchdog confirmed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in the Middle East have been damaged and destroyed by Iran.One of the photos showed a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Saudi Arabia that has been ripped in half, its tail section crumpled into a tangled mess of metal.The images were published on the heels of a report from the Pentagon's watchdog, which found Iranian strikes had "damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict".It also noted that equipment losses have totalled $3.7bn (£2.8bn). Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (£24.7bn) on the war up to 29 June, the report said.In the months after the war began, "dozens of US aircraft were destroyed or damaged", the report continues.The document lists several of the aircraft damaged, including five refuelling aircraft which were "damaged or destroyed on the ground in Saudi Arabia by Iranian munitions".A separate report , externalfrom the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) notes that the E-3 aircraft is no longer in production and would have to be replaced with a more modern equivalent, the E-7.The CBO noted that the E-3 aircraft alone costs $500m (£371m), and the estimated  total cost of equipment lost in battle - including planes, drones and a terminal high altitude area defence system - amounts to $1.9b (£1.4b).CBO said that its review was subject to "uncertainty" because the defence department did not respond to its requests for information, requiring the agency to rely on government databases and public reports.Additionally, the extent of repairs and rebuilding that the US military plans to do remains unclear, according to the report. Brian Katulis of the Middle East Institute said that while "these costs show how the Trump administration burned through precious military resources without having much to show for it", the greater damage had been to broader US military readiness. "The United States had to divert military assets from Asia to the Middle East, leaving America and its partners in Asia more exposed and vulnerable to China," he said. "In addition, the depletion of US munitions makes Russia more willing to probe vulnerabilities with America's NATO allies and continue its aggressive war against Ukraine."While the US has the financial resources to address the equipment losses, it is already facing budgetary problems and may not be able to do so fast enough to prepare for potential flare-ups in the Middle East or elsewhere in the world, he added.Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country.Since the war began Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel.On Tuesday night, the US House of Representatives voted for the third time to end the war in Iran, approving a measure that would force President Donald Trump to end US military action without congressional approval. The vote passed with the help of several Republicans, in what could be the final House vote on the matter ahead of the US midterm elections in November.It faces an uncertain path to passage - the US Senate has not indicated if it will take up the matter.The same day, outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie announced an attempt to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth as new details emerged about the Iran war's price tag for the US.The Trump administration backed Hegseth, with US attorney general Todd Blanche telling reporters he was "doing a phenomenal job".

schema.headline: Photos show widespread damage at US sites from Iranian attacks

title: Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings
description: Figure caption, Why is Donald Trump so opposed to regulating AI?ByNorth America correspondentAccording to Donald Trump, concerns about the dangers of
body: Figure caption, Why is Donald Trump so opposed to regulating AI?ByNorth America correspondentAccording to Donald Trump, concerns about the dangers of artificial intelligence technology – that "robots will be marching into our cities and getting rid of us all" – are a hoax.It's the kind of language the US president typically reserves for the objects of his most intense derision – theories about human-driven climate change, investigations into Russian election-meddling, and the drives to impeach and remove him from office during his first presidential term.Styling himself as the "hoax buster", in a series of social media posts on Monday he issued a full-throated endorsement of what he called "the greatest economic development engine in history" and scorned those who doubted the benefits of the technology.The ranks of doubters have been growing in recent weeks, however, amidst anxiety over the disruptive nature of AI - if not worries about potentially civilisation-threatening danger - among some industry insiders and politicians, including from within Trump's own Republican Party.None of that has deterred Trump, however, whose latest social media fusillade was only his latest effort to turn back growing AI scepticism through sheer force of will. Whether the president views the AI fight as pivotal to his economic legacy, a key battleground in a global struggle for power, or another example of his enemies conspiring against him, he has, by fully joining the fight, elevated the issue to the forefront of American politics. That is even at the risk of crossing longtime allies."We think this could be a great technology, but we're not going to give these guys a carte blanche," former Trump adviser Steve Bannon said at a "pro-human" conference on the dangers of AI on Tuesday. "There's been no debate."Just before Bannon spoke, democratic socialist Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont told the same crowd that Washington policymakers had not addressed the "potentially catastrophic consequence" of unregulated AI."Congress under both Democratic and Republican control has been asleep at the wheel," he said. "And now we have a president whose ignorance regarding this issue is truly embarrassing."Figure caption, Watch: "Great" or "alarming" - Should AI be reined in?According to Trump, however, what's needed isn't debate or new policies, it's trust in his authority and judgement."The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades," he wrote. "We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies."A desire for centralised presidential authority is a familiar theme for Trump in his second term in office. If he decides something is good, he should have the authority to allow it; if he deems it bad, he ought to be able to end it by unilateral presidential order.It's similar to his outlook on immigration and trade. He believes that he, as president, should have the sole power to decide who can enter and remain in the country, and when and where to impose tariffs.Unlike tariffs and immigration, which have been issues of interest for Trump for decades, the rise in artificial intelligence technology is a recent development.But if this is no long-time, deep-seated interest on the part of the president, what could explain his willingness to press ahead?The 'hottest' economy and the driving force of AITrump regularly likes to tout America as the "hottest" country in the world. Many economists indicate that investment in AI technology – including infrastructure and equipment – has been the driving force in the US economy for several years. According to a recent report by the forecasting firm ING, tech investment accounted for more than a third of all US economic expansion in the second quarter of 2026.The stock market is booming, and much of that rise in corporate value (and, by extension, surging retirement portfolios of many Americans) can be attributed to the massive spending on computer chips, data centres and the other infrastructure behind AI.Anything that threatens this growth, which Trump considers to be a hallmark of his presidency and a key to his political legacy, quickly draws his suspicion.Trump also sees the AI expansion as a large-scale industrial competition between the world's two largest economies, the US and China. In the zero-sum game of global power, if China is ahead, then America is behind."We're leading China in AI," Trump said on Saturday, "and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins."The president often touts a familiar conservative view that his opponents on the left are against the free market and economic liberties, and rely on alarmism to justify greater government intervention and control.Of course, Trump – who touts partial US ownership of US Steel and the semiconductor manufacturer Intel, and has no qualms about picking winners and losers in the American economy – is hardly a traditional small-government conservative.Tech bosses vary in views - and their access to TrumpTrump's close ties to prominent tech moguls and AI entrepreneurs from the start of his second term may also help explain his AI evangelism. Tech entrepreneur David Sacks, a co-chair of the president's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology and his informal AI tsar, has been a longtime supporter. Sacks's publicly aired scepticism of AI regulation mirrors recent comments made by the president."I think this is becoming a panic," he said this weekend in an interview with CBS News. "We're in an election season, and there is an incentive for political actors to try and amplify the fear."Elon Musk, despite a rocky relationship, has shaped the direction of this administration. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook, Amazon's Jeff Bezos, OpenAI's Sam Altman and former Apple head Tim Cook all had prominent seats at Trump's inauguration.These men, along with Anthropic head Dario Amodei, hold a range of views on the necessity of greater AI regulation, and have differing levels of access to, and influence on, Trump.In Amodei's case, his conflicts over the Pentagon's unrestricted use of Anthropic's AI models could have negatively affected Trump's evaluation of Amodei's calls for a slowdown in AI development."This is the most prominent debate in the entire industry and has been since the beginning," said Matt Calkins, head of the tech firm Appian. "We knew it would spill into politics at some point because it had to."Figure caption, Watch: AI needs a 'brake pedal', Anthropic co-founder tells BBCWhere the political debate goes from here is an open question.With Trump's resistance, it is unlikely that Congress – despite promises of new hearings and proposed regulatory controls – will enact new legislation that Trump would sign into law. On Tuesday, Republican Speaker of the House Mike Johnson appeared to back away from earlier openness to congressional action, instead echoing Trump "AI hoax" rhetoric.With midterm congressional elections looming, candidates running for office – both Republicans and Democrats – are wary of ending up on the wrong side of public opinion that, according to polls, is sceptical of the promised benefits of AI advances.But Republicans are also wary of crossing Trump on an issue that has become a political touchstone for the president.Even though the public is starting to pay attention, Calkins says that the issue has not yet become political dynamite, which means political rhetoric comes with little risk. The moment when AI warnings turn into a high-profile disaster, however, could be looming."It is possible that events in the future might electrify the public, and then positions - and talk - might not be so cheap," he said.Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

schema.headline: Why Trump is all-in on AI despite the warnings

title: David Gray: Hibernian sack head coach after six league games
description: Hibernian have sacked head coach David Gray six games into the Scottish Premiership season, ending the former captain's 12-year stay at Easter Road.Tu
body: Hibernian have sacked head coach David Gray six games into the Scottish Premiership season, ending the former captain's 12-year stay at Easter Road.Tuesday's 1-0 defeat by bottom-of-the-table Kilmarnock leaves the Edinburgh club ninth in the table on six points.It was Hibs' sixth successive home league loss, stretching back to last season.Assistants Liam Craig and Craig Samson are also leaving, with John Potter placed in charge for Saturday's home game with Aberdeen."Ultimately, this is a decision that we have not taken lightly, but unfortunately, one as a board we had to make due to the recent downturn of results and performances," said executive chairman, Ian Gordon.Gray famously led Hibs to Scottish Cup victory in 2016, heading in a stoppage-time winner against Rangers at Hampden to end a 114-year wait for a third success in the tournament.Having signed two years previously, the right-back retired in 2021 after 177 appearances and joined the coaching staff.After three shorts spells as interim manager, Gray took on the position of head coach in May 2024, replacing Nick Montgomery.He won just one of his first 15 league games but the team staged a remarkable recovery to finish third, while Hibs were fifth last season.Both campaigns yielded European qualifiers which ended in dramatic, last-gasp Conference League play-off exits. Gray oversaw 107 games, winning 43, losing 35 and drawing 29. He departs with a League Cup semi-final against derby rivals Hearts to come on 1 November."Dave has been an inspirational figure at the club during his time here, and he has been a true friend and fantastic colleague to so many," added Gordon."On behalf of my family, I would like to personally thank him for everything he has done for us since we joined the club."As a person, he constantly set the standard with his attitude, professionalism and general work ethic and he will be sorely missed around the building by all the players and staff."On the pitch, he has delivered some incredible moments for our fans, and brought a level of stability and consistency that we haven't reached in recent years."Darren: Sad to see Davey Gray go but correct decision. The writing has been on the wall for a long time. We need to be like Motherwell and Hearts and look outside of Scotland and find a manger with an exciting style of play and fresh ideas. No "old school" Scottish manager!Robbie: It was a great run for David. But I think his time was up after the final whistle went last night. Not a great home run.John: I would like to thank David for what he achieved for the club as a player and then coach with  two decent seasons culminating in European football. The lack of drive, effort and leadership from the players this season has got him the sack. Good luck and thanks for May 2016.Colin: It's a sad day. It felt inevitable after last night though. I wish David Gray all the best. I hope we take a modern approach to finding a new coach and don't go down the route of Malky's contact bookCallum: Unfortunately its all about results and we haven't achieved them with ultimately the highest paid squad in years i think the board need a trusted and experienced manager now.Richard: David Gray is unfortunate - as he is only part of the issue. Malky Mackay [sporting director] should be sacked too - they are members of the same management team and bear equal responsibility.Ben: We got lucky in the end with Gray. After a horrendous start he pulled it back and gave us a third place finish with back to back European qualification. The football and system played however has not been good enough. There is something sad about a club legend coming to thank the fans and instead getting booed, but there was no longer any positives to take, even for the happy clappers.Sam: As a Hearts fan, I'm genuinely sorry to see David Gray sacked. He served Hibs well. I realise that he has to take the rap for the results, but the real truth is that at the moment his players simply aren't very good. These are lean times for Hibs, but they'll come again.Josh: If Hibs could sack Pat Stanton and Frank Sauzee they were always going to sack a Scottish Cup winning David Gray.  You see some of the dross in their back line and realise he had no chance of survival. Poor guy.Alex: Sorry it came to that for David and wish him all the best, unfortunately the manager takes the hit. But the players have let him down time after time, clearly not good enough.

schema.headline: David Gray: Hibernian sack head coach after six league games

title: Ed Sheeran row: How being music's Mr Nice Guy contributed to biggest crisis of his career
description: Figure caption, Will Ed Sheeran cancel his tour as support acts quit?ByMusic correspondentSinger Ed Sheeran is facing the biggest controversy of his c
body: Figure caption, Will Ed Sheeran cancel his tour as support acts quit?ByMusic correspondentSinger Ed Sheeran is facing the biggest controversy of his career after a storm over a decision to drop support act Macklemore from his US stadium tour following the rapper's on-stage pro-Palestinian comments.Sheeran is one of the most successful songwriters of all time. He has sold more than 120 million records and spent more than 1,000 weeks on the US album charts.Part of his appeal - apart from those insidiously catchy songs - is his everyman persona. He looks and dresses like a fan on the train home from Glastonbury, rather than one of the festival's headliners.He has carefully cultivated a non-threatening, everyone welcome public image. In 2014, he donated his entire wardrobe to charity shops. The same year, he adopted a one-month-old kitten, saving it from euthanasia, and named it Graham. Today, he runs a charity providing music lessons to under-18s in his home county of Suffolk.He tries to stay out of politics - usually only getting involved to campaign for issues like copyright protection and ticket touting, or to raise concerns over the impact of Brexit on touring musicians.But like most artists, he leans left. In 2017, he said he supported then-Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, despite not endorsing him at the stump."People thought that, because I didn't put myself behind him, I wasn't a Corbyn supporter," Sheeran told the Sunday Times. "If you knew me as a person, and listened to my music, you would be able to make a pretty educated guess that he would be the kind of person I really dig."When it comes to non-musical issues, Sheeran prefers to remain circumspect. His reasoning, he says, is that music should unite. He views his concerts as a "place of safety and sanctuary" built on shared humanity.This week, that argument has come crumbling down - creating a crisis for his reputation and career.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ed Sheeran performing with Macklemore at the iHeartRadio Music Festival in 2014By now, you probably know the story. Macklemore was picked as opening act on Sheeran's US tour, and on the first night made a speech saying "Free Palestine" and showing images of the destruction in Gaza.The following night, he referred to the death toll as a genocide, a claim that Israel rejects.He faced condemnation, with the organisation StopAntisemitism accusing Macklemore of "ambushing" the audience. Stadium owners, apparently led by the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots, Robert Kraft, put pressure on Sheeran and his promoters to drop him from the tour.After a week of backroom discussions, they got their way.On Tuesday, Sheeran issued a statement saying the decision was made by the promoters, not by him.He said he had tried to build bridges between the parties, to no avail. And he said he was "not complicit", arguing that his decision to remain out of the Middle East debate in public wasn't proof he "didn't care"."I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine," he wrote. "The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy. There are too many wars across the world causing immeasurable pain, none of which should be tolerated."He continued: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds."The statement landed with a thud.If Sheeran is so concerned about children, critics said, how come he hasn't mentioned the thousands of children killed in Gaza?Others pointed out that his abstention from politics was not absolute. He wore a "justice for Grenfell" T-shirt at Wembley Stadium in 2018 after the Grenfell Tower fire, played the Concert For Ukraine in 2022, and recorded a protest song about the Ukraine war with U2 earlier this year.Questions were also raised about his relationship with Kraft. Sheeran sang at the businessman's wedding in 2022, and in a subsequent interview called him "super sweet".Music journalist Jeffrey Ingold said Sheeran's apparent acceptance of the decision to drop Macklemore seemed like "cowardice"."He is one of the biggest musicians in the world," Ingold told BBC Radio 5 Live. "He has power and he has leverage. And he has essentially washed his hands and said, this is not my responsibility."He had options, right? He could have said to the promoters and the owners of the venues, including Robert Kraft, 'You know what, we're not going to do the shows there. If you're not going to let us all perform, we're not going to do it'. He could have found alternate venues."Hours after Sheeran's statement landed, his tour went into crisis. All three support acts for the remaining shows - Finneas, Aaron Rowe and Lukas Graham - pulled out, voicing support for Macklemore. Beoga - who back Sheeran to play songs like Galway Girl and Nancy Mulligan - also quit.Many of them said Macklemore's axing, at the hands of a group of billionaire venue owners, represented a chilling effect on free speech.Others from music and beyond have spoken out. Pop star Pink, who is Jewish, reposted an anti-Macklemore meme and then her own message, explaining why she was critical of the rapper's comments.Suddenly, against his will, Sheeran has become the centre of a political storm over one of the world's most divisive issues.Image source, A. Perez Meca/ Getty ImagesCould Sheeran have handled it better when the controversy blew up? Absolutely.In his statement, he said he wanted to continue the tour, to avoid letting down fans and the crew who rely on his concerts to make a living.If he had threatened to pull the plug on the shows, he could have framed it as a protest for free speech - although that would still inevitably have been interpreted as an endorsement of Macklemore's statements.So, Sheeran stumbled into a Catch 22 situation. He was damned either way.His nice guy image has taken a huge dent, and the "not my responsibility" tone of his statement certainly didn't help.Ingold says: "I think it will change the way people look at him and see him from this point forward."He has said he's not complicit, but he actually is incredibly complicit in what's happening [on this tour]."Jem Aswad, executive music editor of Variety, says the episode shows "you can't be neutral on this issue" - but points out that most people don't go to Sheeran's concerts to be reminded of issues like Gaza, "they go there to stop thinking about it and be entertained".Aswad doubts that this controversy will cause his career major damage, saying he doesn't think most of the criticism "is necessarily coming from Ed Sheeran's fans"."It's coming from people who object to the way that he's behaved in this [situation], and I'm not sure a lot of those people are really Ed Sheeran's fans."We'll find out when Sheeran plays his next show in Philadelphia on Saturday. A vocal contingent might make their thoughts known, but many will just be turning up to enjoy the music.The loss of his backing band isn't the disaster it may seem, either.On previous tours, Sheeran has been the only artist on stage - accompanying himself on a loop pedal instead of relying on other musicians.But once this run of concerts ends in Mexico this December, his next steps will have to be carefully planned.Perhaps, in an age of febrile discontent, staying above the fray is simply impossible.Get in touchAre you an Ed Sheeran fan? Get in touch.

schema.headline: Ed Sheeran row: How being music's Mr Nice Guy contributed to biggest crisis of his career

title: South East businesses speak about the impact of retail crime
description: A shop owner has described how she locks her door during opening hours and customers have to ring the bell to get in after her store was targeted by t
body: A shop owner has described how she locks her door during opening hours and customers have to ring the bell to get in after her store was targeted by thieves last year.Paige Mengers, who runs a designer boutique in Surrey, has been speaking about the impact of shoplifting, with recorded offences remaining above pre-pandemic levels.Home Office figures show there were 42,674 shoplifting offences across Kent, Surrey and Sussex in 2025/26 compared with 28,048 cases in 2019/20.The government said overall offences in England and Wales fell 4% last year, with more suspects being charged.Mengers, who has stores in Cobham and south-west London, said she boosted security after a raid in January 2025 involving men with wire cutters. "One barricaded the door, the other came in and cut the wires on the bags and stole quite a lot of them," she said."It was absolutely awful, I lost two very good members of staff who were terrified after that."We were really shaken and for about six months I had security on the doors for our staff."The borough commander for Elmbridge Chris Thoday told BBC South East the tactics used by these groups were "pretty sophisticated"."They're very organised, they know exactly what they are doing," he said."Quite often they will recce the shops beforehand, then go in afterwards, steal the items they want to take, to make sure they're in and out as quickly as possible."Insp Thoday said a number of stores had since trialled the use of lone worker alarms for staff working alone at night in a number of shops in Cobham. Businesses are sharing their experiences of shop theft as a BBC investigation reveals 270 people were connected to more than 28,000 offences across England. Official data shows 23 per cent of investigations across England and Wales led to a charge or summons in the 12 months up to April this year.It's not just high street stores being targeted, rural areas are also affected.Bosses at a family-run farm shop in Wingham, near Canterbury in Kent, said they had suffered thousands of pounds of losses in a year."We're getting small gangs come in or individuals to steal high value goods, either meat products, meat joints or alcohol," said Andrew Gibson, director at Gibson's Farm Shop."They seem to be more organised, out here you have to drive here, you can't be an opportunist thief."Gibson recently turned to social media to shame offenders online."We've had the situation where thieves have gone back into a police station with the money for the goods to pay back to us," he said.In Canterbury, Kent Police have set up a dedicated retail crime team."People are going in, stealing to order, filling up trolleys and just running out of the stores," said James, a plain clothed police officer speaking to BBC South East during an operation to catch thieves.He said crime groups would sometimes scope out stores and film items they wanted stolen, before sending shoplifters in."We notice people coming in checking out where the CCTV cameras are," he said."Sometimes a shoplifter will use trolleys, they'll load up what they want to take and then they'll hover by the entrance or exit and when the opportunity comes they just take the whole trolley load of goods."We've also noticed people with prams loading up the bottom or the top, wandering around pretending they are getting something out for the young child in the pram and then load up the pram and take items out of the store."Paul Stoner, district commander for police in the city, said the team was set up as a response to a rise in crime over an 18-month period."It's a set few individuals who commit a disproportionate amount of that crime," he said."Our officers have a really good knowledge of the local offenders, we are able to identify them very quickly through the CCTV images," he said."What we also have is the ability to put those images through facial recognition, if the suspect is on a database, we're able to identify them."Police also share information with the local City Watch scheme and details about known suspects can be relayed on a radio system to shops.It's run by the Canterbury Business Improvement District (Bid) and links up retailers with the police and the city council's CCTV control centre.Lisa Carlson, chief executive of Canterbury Bid, said they had a street team which trained businesses, helping them gather and submit evidence."We have 137 radios in circulation, if there is an incident unfolding it can be reported in real time and hopefully we can avoid any crime happening," she said.

schema.headline: South East businesses speak about the impact of retail crime

title: VAR controversy: Pressure for quick decisions obvious in rushed derby review
description: "Quick, quick, quick, quick! Go, go, go, go, go!"The words of video assistant referee Matt Donohue as he rushed through the review to award Erling Haa
body: "Quick, quick, quick, quick! Go, go, go, go, go!"The words of video assistant referee Matt Donohue as he rushed through the review to award Erling Haaland's winning goal in the Manchester derby.No doubt Donohue was simply trying to be as efficient as possible, but it led to one of the most catastrophic VAR errors the Premier League has seen. Donohue and his assistant VAR, Blake Antrobus, inexplicably failed to notice that Enzo Fernandez was three yards offside before he tried to head the ball.The goal was given, and Manchester City beat Manchester United 1-0. Refereeing has always been a goldfish bowl of scrutiny and pressure, heightened by the introduction of VAR.The Premier League made a "more efficient application of VAR to reduce delays" one of its football principles for the season.Has the game tried to prioritise speed over accuracy? The urgency in Donohue's voice was all too apparent. "Let's go, let's go, let's go, let's go!"It was a panicked exchange between the VAR and the replay operator. Not calm, collected and methodical. Rushed and chaotic. The opposite of how a video official should operate.Officials hear repeatedly - from fans, pundits, radio phone-ins and newspaper columns - that VAR has to be quicker. That delays are not acceptable.In the Premier League stakeholders' survey - which includes managers, coaches and supporters - the key theme for improvements to VAR was the speed of decisions.This has to create pressure - but it is no excuse for such an error.City boss Enzo Maresca had some sympathy speaking on Wednesday, though he was of course the beneficiary of the gaffe."To make a decision in 10, 20 seconds is not easy for them," said Maresca. "Sometimes they make mistakes. I make mistakes, players make mistakes. It's part of our job."Referees' chief Howard Webb has taken the desire for quicker reviews on board, but it is still a balancing act.There has been a positive impact, as far as the stats go.VAR delays - including the referee making an announcement to the crowd - have been reduced, from an average of 46 seconds per game to 36 seconds season-on-season. Yet the only other VAR mistake, the failure to award a penalty to Arsenal at Aston Villa, also arguably came about because the incident was cleared too quickly.Completing a VAR review in the shortest possible time is not about skipping steps. And it was a critical mistake by Donohue and Antrobus.Speed is a factor, but the most serious error in process came before Donohue tried to rush through the attacking phase.Donohue asked the replay operator to stop the video on the first replay when Josko Gvardiol touched the ball to cross into the area. He then went immediately into the semi-automated offside technology.This should not have happened.The VAR team should have assessed the full picture, from the playing of the cross to the head of Haaland. This would have provided awareness of Fernandez's position and impact.They did not, and the events inside the penalty area were not considered until the attacking phase was looked at.By then, all that mattered to Donohue and Antrobus was whether Fernandez touched the ball. This would have created a new phase and placed Haaland offside. Donohue has received much of the criticism, but arguably Antrobus' involvement, or lack of, was just as influential.The AVAR's contribution to the entire review was to utter "no, yeah" about the potential touch by Fernandez. This was one second before Donohue uttered the words "final decision is goal, check complete".Antrobus' role is to provide the checks and balances, to make sure the VAR has not missed anything. This fell short. There has been only one lengthy VAR delay this season, in the game between Brentford and Sunderland. A Dan Ballard goal was ruled out for a subjective offside against Kevin Danso.Antrobus was the AVAR in this game, too. There was a great deal of criticism in some parts of the media for that delay, which took over four minutes.Could that have played on Antrobus' mind on Sunday? We cannot know for sure. Ironically, Antrobus played a crucial role in steering VAR Tim Wood to the correct offside decision against Danso. There is also the role of the support VAR, who sits in the operations room next to the match hub at Stockley Park and can intervene on points on protocol.Aware of what was unfolding with the review, no action was taken.It would still have been salvageable in the period between the goal being scored and the kick-off.Pro Ref has placed a huge level of training and resources into VAR in an attempt to make it as efficient and accurate as possible.But when an error of this magnitude happens, no amount of investment can mask the failure. There have been calls to appoint VAR specialists, yet this is exactly what Donohue is - in the Premier League's definition. Three seasons ago, Pro Ref asked for candidates interested in becoming video officials. All those who applied were put through aptitude tests. About 15 made it through to the final stages of training, of which 10 have officiated games in the Premier League.One of those is Donohue, who on Sunday was the video official for the 65th time.Such as been Donohue's development that he is now on the international list, appointed to Uefa club competition qualifying ties over the summer. Donohue has made mistakes, in fact very few do not. It shows how difficult the role is. The only two VARs to have a clear record over the last two seasons are Nick Hopton and Neil Davies, both graduates from the same accelerated programme.Persuading referees to hang up their whistles and spend their professional lives in the VAR room is not easy, nor does it guarantee success.Lee Mason and Mike Dean, the Premier League's only full-time VARs appointed after retirement, were both dismissed by Webb just a few months into his tenure because of a catalogue of errors.One of the only leagues which has a full team of officials who only act as VARs and never go out on the pitch is Spain's La Liga and second division - yet one glance at the headlines there will tell you the controversy is no different to that in England.At the start of last season the VAR completely missed that a player who scored a goal was in an offside position when the ball was played.Pro Ref will have questions to answer over its processes and why a VAR is rushing so desperately over a review in one of the biggest games of the season.That did not happen when West Ham's stoppage-time equaliser against Arsenal was ruled out last season. It took over four minutes - but the VAR came to the correct outcome.The obsession with speed threatens to undermine all the work behind the scenes. But that feels like a football problem and not one caused solely by the actions of the VAR.
